title.en: The Passion and Resurrection of Jesus Christ

texts.period: Composition: Mark c. 70 CE, Matthew/Luke c. 80-90 CE, John c. 90-110 CE; principal MSS: Codex Sinaiticus (British Library Add MS 43725) and Codex Vaticanus, 4th c.; papyri P52, P75 (2nd-3rd c.)

source.archive: Sefaria / Bible Gateway (KJV) / Codex Sinaiticus online
source.work: Mark 14-16; Matthew 26-28; Luke 22-24; John 18-21; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26 (English: King James Version, 1611, public domain)

summary.en: Jesus shares a last supper with his disciples, is betrayed by Judas, tried before Pilate, crucified at Golgotha, buried in a rock tomb; on the third day women find the tomb empty and the risen Lord appears to his followers — the founding narrative of Christian faith, ritually re-enacted in Eucharist and Holy Week.
summary.zh: 耶穌與門徒共進晚餐，遭猶大出賣，於彼拉多前受審，被釘於各各他，葬於石墓；第三日婦女見墓空，復活之主向門徒顯現——此為基督教信仰之根本敘事，於聖餐與聖週禮儀中年年重演。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition; quoted from public-domain KJV.

passages.text: And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me. Likewise also the cup after supper, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you.
And he saith unto them, Be not affrighted: Ye seek Jesus of Nazareth, which was crucified: he is risen; he is not here: behold the place where they laid him.

texts.canonical_translation: King James Version (1611), public domain; modern critical text: Novum Testamentum Graece (Nestle-Aland 28)

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: THE LAST SUPPER. Jesus enters Jerusalem acclaimed as king on an ass's colt; he eats the Passover meal with the Twelve, predicts his betrayal, and institutes the Eucharist — bread broken 'this is my body', the cup 'this is the new testament in my blood' (the earliest written witness, Paul's 1 Corinthians 11:23-26, preserves the tradition within twenty years of the event). Judas Iscariot has already sold him for thirty pieces of silver; at the supper Jesus identifies him: 'that thou doest, do quickly'. In Gethsemane Jesus prays in agony — 'O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me' — while the disciples sleep; Judas arrives with an armed crowd and betrays him with a kiss. Peter three times denies knowing him before the cock crows; Jesus is tried by night before the high priest, condemned for blasphemy ('Again the high priest asked him... Art thou the Christ?... Jesus said: I am'), and delivered to the Roman procurator Pontius Pilate.

MIDDLE: TRIAL AND CRUCIFIXION. Pilate, finding no fault, tries to release him — even offering the customary Passover pardon — but the crowd chooses Barabbas; Jesus is scourged, crowned with plaited thorns, mocked in purple, and crucified at Golgotha between two thieves, with the titulus 'The King of the Jews'. Darkness covers the land from the sixth to the ninth hour; at the end Jesus cries 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' (Mark 15:34, quoting Psalm 22), gives up the ghost, and the temple veil is torn in two from top to bottom. A centurion confesses: 'Truly this man was the Son of God.' Joseph of Arimathaea buries him in a new rock tomb sealed with a great stone; in Matthew the priests set a watch.

END: THE EMPTY TOMB AND APPEARANCES. On the first day of the week, women come to anoint the body: the stone is rolled back, a young man in white (or in John, the risen Jesus himself) announces: 'He is risen; he is not here.' Mark's gospel — our oldest — ends abruptly at 16:8, the women fleeing in fear and telling no one (verses 16:9-20 are a later addition absent from the oldest manuscripts); Matthew has the risen Christ commission the Eleven on a Galilee mountain ('Go ye therefore, and teach all nations'); Luke adds the Emmaus road, where the risen Lord is known 'in breaking of bread'; John gives Mary Magdalene in the garden ('Touch me not') and the doubting Thomas — 'Reach hither thy finger... be not faithless, but believing'. The forty days of appearances close with the Ascension (Luke 24, Acts 1).

VARIANTS AND RECEPTION. The four passion narratives differ in detail (Matthew: earthquake, saints rising; Luke: Herod, penitent thief; John: seamless robe, water and blood, 'It is finished'); theological interpretation ranged from ransom ('a ransom for many') to sacrifice (Hebrews) to Christus victor. Ritual: the narrative structures the Christian liturgical year — Palm Sunday, Maundy Thursday (foot-washing), Good Friday, the Easter Vigil — and the Eucharist re-presents the Last Supper in every celebration; pilgrimage to Jerusalem's Holy Sepulchre from the 4th century onward.
narrative.zh: 始於榮入聖城；逾越節晚餐中設立聖餐，預言出賣；客西馬尼園禱告後被拿，彼得三度不認主，公會夜審定罪。彼拉多查無罪狀仍判釘刑：受鞭、冠荊、紫袍受辱，於各各他釘於二盜之間，罪狀牌書『猶太人的王』；遍地黑暗，最後呼喊詩篇之言，殿幔裂開，百夫長認信。亞利馬太人約瑟葬之於石墓。七日首日清晨，婦女至墓，石已輥開：『他復活了，不在這裡。』馬可於十六章八節戛然而止（九至二十節為後加）；馬太載加利利大使命，路加載以馬忤斯路上於擘餅時被認出，約翰載抹大拉的馬利亞與多馬觸摸傷痕。四十日顯現後升天。禮儀：聖週與復活節守夜禮重演此敘事，聖餐每主日重現晚餐。

functions: Founding narrative of Christian faith and creeds (died, buried, raised on the third day)
Eucharist: ritual re-presentation of the Last Supper in every liturgy
Liturgical year structure: Holy Week, Easter Vigil, Ascension
Jerusalem pilgrimage: Holy Sepulchre from the 4th c. CE

variants.name: Mark (oldest gospel)
variants.text_tradition: c. 70 CE; ends abruptly at 16:8 in Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus
variants.summary: The starkest telling: no birth narrative, no post-resurrection appearances before the longer ending; emphasis on the cry of dereliction and the fear of the women.

variants.name: Matthew and Luke (redacted versions)
variants.summary: Matthew adds the guards, the earthquake, and the Galilee commission; Luke adds Herod's trial, the penitent thief, Emmaus, and the Ascension — both soften Mark's abruptness.

variants.name: John (theological version)
variants.summary: Jesus carries his own cross, gives his mother to the Beloved Disciple, speaks the seven last words; resurrection appearances merge recognition with faith ('blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed').

variants.name: Non-canonical Gospel of Peter (2nd c.)
variants.summary: The cross itself speaks and walks from the tomb; a giant risen Jesus and a walking cross are witnessed by Roman soldiers — an early independent variant showing the range of second-century retellings.

primary_sources.work: Mark 14-16 (with parallels Matthew 26-28, Luke 22-24, John 18-21; 1 Cor 11:23-26)
primary_sources.citation: Novum Testamentum Graece (NA28); English KJV 1611. Key MSS: Codex Sinaiticus (BL Add MS 43725), Codex Vaticanus, P75.

secondary_sources.work: Raymond E. Brown, The Death of the Messiah
secondary_sources.citation: Brown 1994, New York: Doubleday (Anchor Bible Reference) — the standard commentary on the passion narratives and their differences.

secondary_sources.work: Adela Yarbro Collins and John J. Collins, King and Messiah as Son of God
secondary_sources.citation: Yarbro Collins 2008, Grand Rapids: Eerdmans — royal-Davidic framing of the passion title 'King of the Jews'.

source_urls.description: Codex Sinaiticus online facsimile (British Library) — Mark 14-16, earliest witness to the abrupt ending

texts.sensitivity_guidance: Canonical scripture of a living faith: cite by chapter/verse from established editions; avoid casual remixing; be aware of Jewish-Christian polemical history of the passion narrative when excerpting trial scenes.

title.en: The Creation of Adam and the Fall of Iblis (Quran)
title.zh: 阿丹之造與易卜劣廝之墮（古蘭經）

region.zh: 麥加／麥地那（誦經語境；象徵性定位）

texts.period: Quran revealed c. 610-632 CE; canonical rasm fixed under Uthman (c. 650 CE); earliest MSS: Sanaa palimpsest, Codex Parisino-petropolitanus (1st c. AH); tafsir tradition from al-Tabari (d. 923 CE)

source.work: Quran 2:30-39; 7:11-25; 15:26-48; 20:115-127; 38:71-85 (Arabic text; English: E. H. Palmer, The Qur'an, Sacred Books of the East vol. 6, Oxford 1880)

texts.license: Arabic text public domain; Palmer 1880 translation public domain

summary.en: God creates Adam from clay, teaches him the names of all things, and the angels bow — all but Iblis, who refuses ('I am better than he') and is cast down until the Day of Judgment; Adam and his wife dwell in the Garden, approach the forbidden tree through Satan's whispering, and are sent down to earth, where revealed words teach them repentance.
summary.zh: 真主以黏土造阿丹，教以萬物之名，天使皆拜——惟易卜劣廝拒拜（『我比他尊貴』），遂被逐，待至審判日；阿丹夫婦居園中，受魔鬼唆使近禁樹，被降於大地，得啟示之言而悔悟。

sensitivity.note: The Quran is the literal word of God in Arabic; translations are interpretations. Only public-domain translations are quoted, with the Arabic source as primary.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Quran 2:30-33 (Palmer 1880 translation): The Lord says to the angels, 'I am going to place in the earth a successor'; they ask whether he will place one who will do evil there while they praise God; He teaches Adam the names of all things and calls the angels to name them — 'did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and of the earth?' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Quran 2; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Quran 7:11-18: God commands the angels to bow before Adam; all bow except Iblis, who says 'I am better than he: Thou hast created me from fire and him from clay.' God casts him down: 'Get out of it, despised, driven away'; Iblis obtains respite until the Day of Judgment, vowing to lie in wait for Adam's children. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Quran 7; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: E. H. Palmer, The Qur'an, Sacred Books of the East vol. 6, Oxford 1880 (public domain); modern: Sahih International, Abdel Haleem (copyright)

narrative.en:
The Quran retells the Adam story not as one continuous sura but as a cycle of episodes spread across Meccan and Medinan revelations, each re-focusing the tale on obedience, knowledge, and the enmity of Iblis.

THE CREATION AND THE NAMES. God announces to the angels: 'I am going to place in the earth a khalifa (successor/viceroy)' (2:30). The angels object — will this creature 'do evil therein and shed blood, while we celebrate thy praise?' God's answer is an act of teaching: He 'taught Adam the names, all of them' (2:31) — the names of all things, the gift of language and knowledge no angel possesses — and when the angels fail the test, God calls Adam to recite them: 'Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and of the earth?' (2:33). Adam is created from sounding clay (salsal), from mud kneaded (15:26); in the tafsir tradition (al-Tabari, citing Ibn Abbas) the clay is gathered from every earth — white, black, red, sweet, bitter — so that Adam's children will be of every kind.

THE REFUSAL OF IBLIS. God commands the angels to prostrate before Adam. All bow except Iblis — 'he refused and was arrogant, and was of the disbelievers' (2:34). His reason: 'I am better than he: Thou hast created me from fire and him from clay' (7:12). The refusal is the Quran's primal sin: pride of substance over obedience. God casts him out — 'Get thee down from it, despised and driven away' (7:18) — and Iblis obtains respite until the Day of Judgment, on which he vows to 'lie in wait for them upon thy straight path' (7:16), to tempt Adam's children 'from before them, behind them, from their right and from their left'. God grants the respite: 'over my servants thou shalt have no power' except those who follow him (15:42-43).

THE GARDEN AND THE TREE. Adam dwells with his spouse in the Garden, eating freely 'wherever ye will' — but not 'this tree', approached lest they 'be of the unjust doers' (2:35). Satan (al-Shaytan, Iblis) whispers that the tree is 'the tree of eternity' (20:120), that eating will make them angels or immortal; the two eat, 'and their shame became apparent to them, and they began to stitch upon themselves leaves of the garden' (7:22). Unlike the biblical telling, the Quran distributes the transgression to both (the couple, not the wife alone), and the serpent plays no speaking role: the tempter is Iblis himself. Both are stripped, both descend.

THE DESCENT AND THE WORDS OF REPENTANCE. The fall is answered by mercy: 'Adam received words from his Lord, and He turned toward him, for He is the Relenting, the Compassionate' (2:37) — in the tafsir tradition, the words are those of sura 7:23 ('Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves') or a divine prayer of repentance. Adam is set down on earth 'a dwelling and a provision' (2:36) — the human condition as exile-with-mercy, not inherited guilt: 'no soul shall bear the burden of another' (6:164). The episode closes with the promise of guidance ('there shall surely come to you guidance from me; whoso followeth my guidance, no fear shall be on them') — prophecy itself is the sequel to the fall.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Islamic theology of human nature (fitra — no original sin), the protocol of angels' obedience, the taxonomy of pride (takabbur) as the first sin, and the ritual of repentance (tawba); it is recited at weddings and funerals in various regions and is the anchor for the Muslim etiquette of resisting satanic whispering (isti'adha before recitation).
narrative.zh: 古蘭經以多處經文重述阿丹之事：真主告眾天使將於大地設『代治者』；天使問將置造惡流血者乎；真主教阿丹萬物之名，天使不能名。真主命天使拜阿丹，易卜劣廝自恃火造優於土造而拒拜，遂被逐，求緩刑至審判日，誓誘惑阿丹子孫。阿丹夫婦居園中得食園果，惟近禁樹勿為；魔鬼唆言此樹致永生，二人食之，羞恥乃現，以園葉蔽身。真主降諭：阿丹獲主之數言而蒙饒恕——無原罪之世，人各負其責。夫婦降於大地為居所與給養，啟示隨之而至：循主之引導者無懼。功能：人性本淨之義、天使順服之儀、傲慢為首罪、悔悟之禮。

functions: Theology of fitra: human nature untainted by original sin
Pride of substance (fire vs. clay) as the first sin — Iblis' refusal
Ritual: isti'adha (seeking refuge from Satan) before recitation; repentance (tawba)
Charter of knowledge: Adam taught 'the names' grounds human epistemic dignity

variants.name: al-Tabari's tafsir (Isra'iliyyat material)
variants.text_tradition: Jami' al-bayan fi ta'wil al-Quran (d. 923 CE); trans. Cooper/Brinner (copyright)
variants.summary: Collects the early exegetical expansions: the clay gathered from the four corners, the hollow Adam left standing while angels feared it, Iblis' entry into the Garden 'in the mouth of the serpent' — traditions inherited from Jewish-Christian sources, weighed critically by Muslim exegetes.

variants.name: Biblical Genesis parallel
variants.summary: Shares the Garden, the tree, the leaf-clothing; differs in the serpent (silent or absent in the Quran), the wife's role (both eat), and the fall (exile-with-mercy rather than inherited curse).

variants.name: Sufi readings (Ibn Arabi and later)
variants.summary: Ibn Arabi reads Iblis' refusal as the lover's exclusive devotion (he would bow to none but God), making the episode a parable of the tension between pure love and revealed command.

variants.name: Popular hagiography (Stories of the Prophets)
variants.summary: Expands into full narrative lore: the four clays, Adam's size (60 cubits), the naming of all things, and the children born after the descent — the story-book Adam that shaped vernacular Islam across Asia.

primary_sources.citation: 2:30-39; 7:11-25; 15:26-48; 20:115-127; 38:71-85. Canonical Uthmanic rasm; earliest MSS: Codex Parisino-petropolitanus (BNF arabe 328), Sanaa palimpsest. English: E. H. Palmer, SBE vol. 6, Oxford 1880 (public domain).

secondary_sources.work: Fazlur Rahman, Major Themes of the Quran
secondary_sources.citation: Rahman 1980, Minneapolis: Bibliotheca Islamica — theological reading of the Adam-Iblis cycle and fitra.

secondary_sources.work: Andrew Rippin (ed.), The Blackwell Companion to the Quran
secondary_sources.citation: Rippin 2006, Oxford: Blackwell — chapters on tafsir and the Isra'iliyyat problem.

Quran.com — Arabic text with multiple translations and verse numbering

texts.sensitivity_guidance: The Quran is the literal word of God in Arabic; translations are interpretations and must be labeled as such. Quote from established translations with sura:verse; never paraphrase the Arabic itself; avoid casual remixing; note that depictions of Adam and Iblis are avoided in many Muslim communities.
